**(2) The motivation of compositional score metrics is not very clear. What's the difference between this work and just defining multiple fine-grained aspects and doing a performance average? Is it necessary to build such a compositional scoring framework?**

The difference between IntegratedScore and simple averaging lies in the fact that it **does not mechanically average multiple fine-grained metrics**, but **instead applies a structured combination rule to reflect the overall quality** of a report. For example, if a report has broad coverage but entirely untrustworthy citations, **a simple average may still yield a moderate score, thereby distorting evaluation**. In contrast, **IntegratedScore explicitly reduces overall credibility, which better aligns with human review logic**. We argue that this framework is necessary, as it **prevents systems from achieving high scores by “gaming” a single dimension, emphasizes multi-dimensional balance, and enhances both interpretability and robustness**. The choice of a multiplicative model rather than a weighted average is grounded in the logic of the “barrel theory” and quality gating: the multiplicative formula ensures that only when content, topical relevance, and credibility are all satisfied can a high score be achieved, **which more faithfully reflects human definitions of high-quality research reports**.  

Furthermore, in designing IntegratedScore, **the three components each serve distinct core functions**: Quality measures task completion and writing quality, SemanticDrift ensures topical focus, and TrustworthyBoost guarantees citation credibility. **Without any one of these, a model may generate topic-relevant but valueless text, high-quality but off-topic reports, or polished writing with untrustworthy references, all of which fail to evaluate the true capabilities of deep research agents**. In our experiments, we observed that removing SemanticDrift allowed off-topic reports to still receive high scores; removing TrustworthyBoost made it impossible to distinguish unreliable citations (mostly unverifiable blogs and posts); and removing Quality eliminated the ability to capture task completion and writing quality, which is the core of deep research. **Indeed, Table 1 presents metric-wise ablation results**: we report the individual scores of Quality, SemanticDrift, and TrustworthyBoost, as well as their combined IntegratedScore. The comparison shows that relying on any single dimension leads to significant biases, whereas **the integrated metric provides a more comprehensive and stable reflection of DRA capabilities**. This analysis demonstrates that **each component is indispensable, and the multiplicative structure of the joint score ensures multi-dimensional constraints and balance**. In addition, we will revisit experimental logs and include a concise ablation analysis with illustrative examples in the camera-ready version to more intuitively demonstrate the necessity of each component.

---

**We sincerely hope the above explanations have resolved any confusion and clarified potential misunderstandings. Your assessment is invaluable to us, and we deeply trust in your professionalism and fairness in making this determination. We once again express our heartfelt gratitude for your affirmation.**

**Affectionate and deep homage,**

**Authors of Submission 20638**

---

> [1] Du, M., Xu, B., Zhu, C., Wang, X., & Mao, Z. (2025). DeepResearch Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Deep Research Agents. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.11763*.
>
> [2] Yifei, L. S., Chang, A., Malaviya, C., & Yatskar, M. (2025). Researchqa: Evaluating scholarly question answering at scale across 75 fields with survey-mined questions and rubrics. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.00496*.
>
> [3] Wan, H., Yang, C., Yu, J., Tu, M., Lu, J., Yu, D., ... & Zhou, D. (2025). DeepResearch Arena: The First Exam of LLMs' Research Abilities via Seminar-Grounded Tasks. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.01396*.
>
> [4] Li, M., Zeng, Y., Cheng, Z., Ma, C., & Jia, K. (2025). Reportbench: Evaluating deep research agents via academic survey tasks. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.15804*.

---

**(2) Experiments focus mainly on current DRAs vs tool-augmented LLMs. It is unclear how robust the benchmark is for future, more diverse systems.**

Although our experiments currently focus on existing Deep Research Agents (DRAs) and tool-augmented LLMs, the design of our benchmark **is fundamentally system-agnostic and does not depend on any specific model or agent implementation**. Its core lies in the definition of tasks and reference bundles, while the rubric dimensions (e.g., structural completeness, logical coherence, coverage depth, citation credibility, and data rigor) **serve as universal standards across systems and scenarios**. We **emphasized scalability and transferability during construction**:  

**(a) Task level**: In the data construction stage, expert guidelines strictly constrained the authority and long-term stability of queries and Trustworthy-Source Links (TSLs). At the metric level, we introduced Hostname Matching and tunable hyperparameters to reduce dependence on specific pages, and for long-term maintenance we commit to regular link validity checks and the incorporation of Internet Archive snapshots, thereby **ensuring stability and generality of the benchmark**.  

**(b) Evaluation level**: The integrated metrics provide a more comprehensive and stable reflection of system capabilities, while the multiplicative scoring structure enforces multi-dimensional constraints and balance. Since these three components are universal requirements across systems and scenarios, IntegratedScore does not rely on any particular implementation, but instead establishes a stable, scalable, and reproducible evaluation baseline for future, more diverse research agents. Thus, the benchmark **remains robust and applicable to future systems**.  

**(c) Robustness validation**: Our experiments already cover 13 different systems, demonstrating that the framework can **fairly compare diverse implementations**. Future systems of greater variety can also be directly integrated into this framework.  

In summary, the robustness of our benchmark is not limited to current DRAs or tool-augmented LLMs; rather, it **provides a stable, scalable, and reproducible evaluation baseline for richer and more diverse systems in the future**.

---

**(3) Figure 2 contains too many abbreviations. They should be explained in the caption at least.**

***(As added in Figure 2 of the rebuttal revision)*** Thank you for your reminder. We agree that the abbreviations in Figure 2 require clearer explanation. In the rebuttal revision, we have **updated the main figure** and **added clearer explanations together with a representative example to facilitate reader understanding**. We will further refine the main figure in the camera-ready version to make it more visually appealing and intuitive.

**It is truly a privilege to engage in these discussions regarding future prospects with a companion with curiosity and desire. We sincerely hope the above explanations have resolved any confusion and clarified potential misunderstandings. Your assessment is invaluable to us, and we deeply trust in your professionalism and fairness in making this determination. We once again express our heartfelt gratitude for your affirmation.**

>
> [2] Yifei, L. S., Chang, A., Malaviya, C., & Yatskar, M. (2025). Researchqa: Evaluating scholarly question answering at scale across 75 fields with survey-mined questions and rubrics. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.00496*.
>
> [3] Wan, H., Yang, C., Yu, J., Tu, M., Lu, J., Yu, D., ... & Zhou, D. (2025). DeepResearch Arena: The First Exam of LLMs' Research Abilities via Seminar-Grounded Tasks. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.01396*.
>
> [4] Li, M., Zeng, Y., Cheng, Z., Ma, C., & Jia, K. (2025). Reportbench: Evaluating deep research agents via academic survey tasks. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.15804*.

---

**(3) The evaluation relies on LLM-as-a-Judge and rubric quality, yet provides little analysis of judgment reliability or rubric coverage, which are crucial to the claimed rigor.**

***(As added in Appendix B.7 of the rebuttal revision)*** In our experiments, we conducted human consistency validation of the reliability of LLM judgments: 35% of the samples were randomly selected and independently scored by experts, and **the results showed a 99.3% consistency with LLM judgments (as in lines 449–450)**, which demonstrates that LLM-as-Judge is **reliable in this setting**. **This high consistency is largely attributable to the rigorous design of our rubrics**, whose scoring rules remain **highly precise and explicit**, thereby **avoiding misjudgments** caused by model subjectivity. Furthermore, the rubric design process was grounded in **expert-defined task objectives**, ensuring **coverage of key dimensions**, and **included multiple rounds of independence checks**, both human and LLM-based, during the design stage **to prevent redundancy or overlap**. For details on rubric coverage, please refer to Appendix B.5 for Query-Specific Rubrics (QSRs) and Appendix B.2 for General-Report Rubrics (GRRs).

---

**(4) The benchmark’s filtering with o4-mini-deep-research may introduce systematic bias by excluding tasks it handles poorly.**

We use o4-mini-deep-research, a well-known model, as a baseline to **filter out overly simple** (**in fact, trivially high-performing rather than poorly performing**), **clearly invalid, or duplicate tasks**, thereby retaining high-difficulty problems to ensure benchmark quality rather than to evaluate reasoning depth. Moreover, o4-mini-deep-research serves only as an auxiliary tool during construction and **is not the criterion for deciding task retention**. As shown in Figure 2, the final set **is determined through Stage 3 manual review and Stage 6 manual cross-review to ensure that no task category is systematically excluded due to any single model’s weaknesses**. We provide task distribution statistics in Section 3.1 and Appendix B.1, demonstrating **broad and balanced coverage of task types**.

---

**(5) The 48-item General-Report Rubrics embed subjective formatting assumptions that may not always necessary or universally applicable, with similar concerns for task-specific rubrics.**

***(As added in lines 195-198 of the rebuttal revision)*** The General-Report Rubrics (GRRs) constitute a **necessary, objective, and broadly applicable set of standards that define the fundamental expectations of humans for report-style responses**. A qualified report must not only accomplish the assigned task but also exhibit structural completeness, logical coherence, sufficient information coverage, credible citations, insightful perspectives, rigorous data analysis, and consistent technical formatting as universal quality requirements. Specifically, GRRs evaluate report quality across seven dimensions, forming **a comprehensive assessment framework built upon the dual pillars of content and expression**. Although a small number of items involve stylistic or opinion-based judgments, these are **intrinsic to the nature of reports**, which are expected **not only to present facts but also to summarize, compare, and draw conclusions**. Complementing GRRs, the Query-Specific Rubrics (QSRs) are constructed around concrete task objectives, **authored by experts**, and **validated through multiple rounds of cross-checking to ensure correctness and coverage of content alignment**. Together, GRRs and QSRs guarantee that reports **meet both task completion requirements and general quality standards**, while the adjustable weighting of the Quality metric allows flexible balancing across different scenarios. This combination establishes a complete, rigorous, and reusable evaluation framework tailored for Deep Research Agents.

---

**(2) In lines 212 - 213, which terms qualify as "prone to triggering topic divergence"?**

***(As added in lines 269-272 of the rebuttal revision)*** In defining Focus-Deviation Keywords (FDKs), we refer to words that are semantically related to the target topic but induce topic drift. For example, when the query focuses on “men’s football matches”, the word “women” may cause the report to deviate from the intended subject. Similarly, when the query centers on the “electric vehicles”, terms such as “fuel cars” or “motorcycles” are categorized as FDKs. During data construction, these words were pre-annotated by an expert team and validated through multiple rounds of cross-review to **ensure consistency and rationality**. The presence of such words indicates that the generated report may contain content inconsistent with the target topic, leading to semantic drift or topic shift. In the costly generation process of DRA models, irrelevant content results in token waste and excessive report entropy.  

Importantly, we do not adopt a blanket assumption that the occurrence of these words necessarily implies topic deviation. Instead, as detailed in Section 4.2, we apply the expectation scaling factor $\epsilon$ together with a minimum-value function for threshold control, combined with contextual semantic relevance assessment. This enables **a more effective and persuasive evaluation of whether topic deviation occurs and whether it leads to costly resource waste**.

---

**(3) Who qualify as "experts" in the data collection process?**

Our data collection and rubric development were conducted by multiple doctoral researchers with systematic academic backgrounds and extensive expertise in artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and information retrieval. Furthermore, the benchmark design encouraged these researchers to contribute domains and topics with which they were deeply familiar. All rubrics were independently formulated by the expert team and subjected to multiple rounds of cross-review and consistency checks to **ensure scientific rigor and reliability**.

---

**(4) In line 269, what exact principles are followed?**

In fact, this point has **already been explained across the subsections** of the same section. The design of Semantic Quality follows the Weighted Average Method (WAM) from Multi-Attribute Decision Making (MADM) (as in lines 305–307), applying ratio normalization to the total scores of QSRs and GRRs. The design of Topical Focus is constructed on the multiplicative relationship between keyword frequency (TF) and semantic relevance, inspired by the TF × IDF model in information retrieval, which suppresses marginal word weights and strengthens topic anchoring (as in lines 326–328). The Retrieval Trustworthiness metric transforms match rates into multiplicative scoring factors to increase the evaluative weight of citation quality, based on the hit rate of TSLs and employing a confidence enhancement mechanism inspired by multiplicative fusion in Bayesian updating (as in lines 352–354).  

The integrated scoring metric adopts a multiplicative weighting model to enable multidimensional evaluation of report-style generation tasks (as in lines 374–375). Analogous to interaction-effect modeling in statistics, the joint metric captures the combined influence across multiple dimensions rather than merely linear aggregation. Moreover, the multiplicative model introduces constraining coupling terms among dimensions, such that a low score in any single dimension suppresses the overall score, thereby aligning more closely with the logic of multidimensional evaluation.

---

**(5) In Section 4.1, how is ratio normalization performed?**

***(As added in lines 315 of the rebuttal revision)*** Ratio normalization is a common and widely used data scaling method, aiming to map the raw scores of different indicators into a fixed interval $[0,1]$ for the purpose of comparison and integration. In Section 4.1, it is defined as:
\[
\mathcal{N}_\text{Ratio}[\cdot] = \frac{\cdot}{\sum_i \mathrm{FullScore}(r_i)}
\]

---

**(6) In lines 363 - 365, to what does the framework scale and transfer, and how is it shown by the Algorithm?**

By “scalability” and “transferability,” we refer to the **framework’s extensibility** across task size and complexity, namely its ability to **maintain scoring stability**. They also denote the **benchmark and framework’s adaptability** across model types, being applicable not only to DRAs but also to other long-text generation systems (e.g., tool-augmented models). This has been demonstrated in our experiments, where the framework was applied to 13 different systems and consistently yielded comparable results. The algorithmic workflow **ensures that outputs from different models and systems can be evaluated under a unified scale**, thereby **reflecting the framework’s scalability and transferability**.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a new deep research benchmark and multidimensional evaluation framework. The benchmark consists of 214 expert-curated queries, each paired with a "reference bundle" that includes: Query-Specific Rubrics (QSRs), General-Report Rubrics (GRRs), Trustworthy Source Links (TSLs), Focus-Anchor Keywords (FAKs), and Focus-Deviation Keywords (FDKs).

On top of these, the benchmark defines a set of quantitative metrics for evaluating report-style outputs along multiple dimensions. The paper evaluates 13 models or agents, including both Deep Research systems and web-search-augmented reasoning models.

strengths.value: A viable attempt to evaluate deep research agents on long-report tasks with carefully designed rubrics and a comprehensive evaluation framework. The construction process is well-documented and the multidimensional scoring design (semantic quality, topical focus, retrieval trustworthiness) is conceptually thorough.

weaknesses.value:
- There has been a surge of recent benchmarks in the deep research domain, several of which already include evaluation of long-form answers, citation accuracy, and rubric-based evaluation. It's suggested to include a table of comparison for  key dimensions (e.g., short answer or report, static or time-varying tasks, evaluation methods). Otherwise it's a bit hard to understand the contribution under the crowded space.
- The main text largely describes the benchmark and evaluation pipeline only in abstract terms. It lacks concrete examples to illustrate task nature and rubric design. At least one representative task example should appear in the main paper rather than only in Appendix B.3, to help readers understand the task more intuitively.
- The evaluation heavily relies on LLM-as-a-Judge to score rubrics (a list of Yes/Partial/No items) and on the quality of both task-specific and meta-level rubrics. However, the paper provides little analysis of the reliability of LLM-based judgments, nor of the coverage or independence of rubric entries themselves. These aspects are crucial to the claimed rigor and would be better to be examined.
- The benchmark construction phase reportedly includes a filtering stage using o4-mini-deep-research, which could introduce systematic bias by excluding certain types of tasks that such a model handles poorly.
- The General-Report Rubrics (48 items) embed many assumptions about ideal formatting and stylistic qualities, yet it is unclear whether these are necessary, objective, or universally desirable criteria. From a quick look, not all tasks or agents should be expected to satisfy all 48 stylistic rules, and several rubric items involve inherently subjective judgments. Similar concerns may apply to the task-specific rubrics.
- The Retrieval Trustworthiness metric appears overly dependent on the provided Trustworthy Source Links (TSLs), even though in many realistic cases alternative credible sources could exist. This dependence may penalize otherwise valid retrievals that fall outside the preselected reference set.
- Overall, the evaluation design lacks sufficient justification, making it difficult to fully trust the results in the main table. Some systems may achieve higher scores simply because they happen to align better with the benchmark’s stylistic or structural expectations. As in prior work (e.g., Du et al., 2025), the scoring mechanism itself is also extremely complex, which further obscures interpretability and robustness.

**(7) The dataset lacks a discussion on how to keep the links up-to-date and how to handle broken links.** 

***(As added in lines 211-253 of the rebuttal revision)*** In contrast to approaches such as DeepResearch Bench [1], ResearchQA [2], DeepResearch Arena [3], and ReportBench [4], which primarily rely on model self-generation and self-judgment and often suffer from high evaluation noise, a common challenge across the field, we adopt a more conservative yet rigorous and persuasive design based on human-curated trustworthy sources. At the current stage, human involvement remains indispensable for establishing a Gold Standard. 

(1) For **data construction**, we explicitly defined in the guideline distributed to experts the requirements for the stability and longevity of queries and Trustworthy-Source Links (TSLs). TSLs must be authoritative, official, primary, stably accessible, and unlikely to change or expire (e.g., government or academic institutions), rather than unstable websites such as forums or blogs that are highly subjective and prone to invalidation. **This ensures the stability of TSLs at the source**; 

(2) For **metric mechanism**, we introduced Hostname Matching (as in Section 4.3) **to reduce dependence on specific pages**. In constructing TrustworthyBoost, we also incorporated hyperparameters that **allow the Full Match to be adjusted** across different evaluation targets **to maintain stability**; 

(3) For **long-term dynamic maintenance**, we commit to **regularly checking link validity** (e.g., quarterly) and plan to **incorporate snapshots** from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine as permanent references. **This ensures that even if pages change or disappear, the benchmark remains reproducible and valid over time**.

---

**(8) The metrics heavily rely on key work (*do you mean keyword?*) matching, which I doubt is suitable for evaluating deep research agents.**

For the Topical Focus metric, SemanticDrift **does not mechanically rely on string matching but instead combines keyword matching with LLM-based semantic relevance judgment**. More importantly, the integrated score is multiplicatively composed of three dimensions: Quality, SemanticDrift, and TrustworthyBoost. A deficiency in any dimension significantly suppresses the overall score, and keyword signals alone cannot dominate the conclusion. **This is also clearly reflected in the metric-wise ablation results**. In Table 1, we report not only the integrated score but also the individual scores of each metric. It can **be directly observed that SemanticDrift, relative to the IntegratedScore, is not a decisive factor and does not heavily dominate**. It is precisely this joint system, where Quality serves as the core, SemanticDrift as a penalizing factor, and TrustworthyBoost as a rewarding factor, that **enables a comprehensive and persuasive evaluation** of DRAs.

---

**(9) The contribution efficiency metric seems to be naturally biased against long responses.**

***(As added in lines 417-423 of the rebuttal revision)*** The design of Contribution Efficiency is **not intended to penalize long texts but rather to measure the information density per token**. If a long text maintains high information density (i.e., every token carries value), the efficiency score can still be high; **the score is only suppressed when the text contains substantial redundancy or off-topic content**, which is precisely what we aim to detect. Therefore, this metric is not a bias but a deliberately designed constraint to encourage models to generate efficient long-form outputs. Moreover, Contribution/Token is only an auxiliary metric: it does not determine the IntegratedScore but instead **helps interpret the cost-effectiveness of the model, especially given that DRAs are generally very expensive**.

summary.value:
This paper proposes Rigorous Bench, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate Deep Research Agents on report-style tasks. 
It contributes 1) a dataset of 214 expert-curated, high-complexity queries across diverse domains, each paired with rich reference bundles,  and 2) a multidimensional evaluation framework capturing semantic quality, topical focus, and retrieval trustworthiness. 
Experiments with 13 models show that DRAs outperform tool-augmented baselines, while highlighting systemic limitations such as efficiency–quality and decomposition–coherence trade-offs.

strengths.value:
- Some prior benchmarks are limited to short-form answers, while this work targets long-form, report-style outputs.
- The dataset design includes expert involvement, multi-stage validation, and inclusion of trustworthy sources.
- Clear evaluation framework with interpretable integrated scoring, not just black-box similarity metrics.
- Experimental results are extensive, covering a variety of strong baselines and providing clear differentiation.

weaknesses.value:
- Heavy reliance on expert-designed rubrics and curated sources may introduce biases and limit scalability.
- Experiments focus mainly on current DRAs vs tool-augmented LLMs. It is unclear how robust the benchmark is for future, more diverse systems.

questions.value: - Fig. 2 contains too many abbreviations. They should be explained in the caption at least.

---

**(6) The Retrieval Trustworthiness metric seems overly dependent on the preselected Trustworthy Source Links, which may penalize valid retrievals from alternative credible sources.**

During the data construction stage, our principle guidelines distributed to experts **explicitly specified requirements for the stability and longevity** of both queries and Trustworthy-Source Links (TSLs). TSLs must represent **the most authoritative, official, and primary sources** of information for answering the query, and they must be stably accessible, resistant to change, and unlikely to expire (e.g., government or academic institution websites), rather than unstable sources such as forums or blogs that are **highly subjective** and prone to disappearance. This design **ensures the stability and representativeness of TSLs from the outset**, and they **can even be regarded as uniquely optimal**. Meanwhile, TrustworthyBoost functions as a rewarding factor that **applies only to primary, verifiable, and official sources (already listed in the TSLs)**. **For non-primary, paraphrased, unverifiable, or non-official sources, it neither increases the integrated score nor imposes penalties**, thereby **ensuring robustness and fairness** in evaluation results.

summary.value: * The paper proposes "Rigorous Bench," a benchmark for Deep Research Agents (DRAs) focusing on long-form, report-style responses. It comprises 214 expert-curated queries across 10 domains. The core contribution is a multidimensional evaluation framework utilizing "reference bundles" (rubrics, keywords, trustworthy links) to assess semantic quality, topical focus, and retrieval trustworthiness, aiming to move beyond simple accuracy metrics.

reviewer_concerns.value:
**Addressed:**

Comparison with related work (Uu5v, 9wgF): The authors added a comparison table (Table R.1) in the appendix to position their work against other recent benchmarks like DeepResearch Arena and ReportBench.

Lack of concrete examples (Uu5v, a7RE): The authors updated Figure 2 and the appendix to include specific task examples and rubric details, which was a major request.

Definitions and Details (9wgF): Clarifications were provided regarding "Focus-Deviation Keywords" and the normalization methods used in scoring.

**Outstanding:**

Fragility and Link Rot (MLBk, 9wgF, Uu5v): This is the most critical unresolved issue. The benchmark relies on a pre-defined set of "Trustworthy Source Links" (TSLs). If these links die or change, the benchmark breaks. The authors' rebuttal promising "quarterly checks" and "hostname matching" does not fully solve the reproducibility crisis inherent in web-based benchmarks, nor does it address the issue that valid information might exist on non-TSL pages (penalizing agents that find correct info elsewhere).

Scoring Complexity vs. Value (MLBk, 9wgF): Reviewers questioned the necessity of the complex multiplicative "Integrated Score" versus simple averaging. The rebuttal argues for a "barrel theory" approach (weakest link determines score), but the complexity of the metric (involving keywords, LLM judges, and link matching) obscures interpretability.

Metric Validity (9wgF, Uu5v): The "Contribution Efficiency" metric potentially penalizes comprehensive reports. Furthermore, while the authors claim 99.3% human-LLM agreement, this figure is surprisingly high for subjective report evaluation, raising questions about the nuance of the validation study which were not fully cleared up.

summary.value: This work claims to introduce a rigorous benchmark for evaluating deep research agents (DRAs) for report style response generation. The dataset spans 10 domains and includes 214 queries. A multi-dimensional evaluation framework is introduced for fine-grained evaluation, focusing on semantic quality, topical focus, and retrieval trustworthiness. Experiments on popular deep research agents as well as language models reveals the strong performance of DRAs and room for further improvement.

**(1) Heavy reliance on expert-designed rubrics and curated sources may introduce biases and limit scalability.**

***(As added in Appendix B.7 of the rebuttal revision)*** We deliberately adopt expert-designed rubrics and manually curated trustworthy sources, following **a more conservative yet rigorous human-centered design to ensure long-term validity**. This approach **guarantees both the rigor and credibility of evaluation**, while also **providing a more practical and realistic assessment aligned with human preferences and expectations**. Fundamentally, this distinguishes our benchmark from DeepResearch Bench [1], ResearchQA [2], DeepResearch Arena [3], and ReportBench [4], which primarily rely on model self-generation and self-judgment and often suffer from high evaluation noise, a common challenge across the field. At the current stage, **human involvement is indispensable for establishing a Gold Standard**. Although our dataset is relatively small, its quality is exceptionally high.  

To **reduce bias**, we conducted multiple rounds of cross-validation in rubric design to **ensure comprehensive coverage and independence of items**. Specifically, the General-Report Rubrics (GRRs) constitute **a necessary, objective, and broadly applicable set of standards** that define the fundamental expectations for report-style responses: a qualified report must not only accomplish the assigned task but also exhibit structural completeness, logical coherence, sufficient information coverage, credible citations, insightful perspectives, rigorous data analysis, and consistent technical formatting. Complementing GRRs, the Query-Specific Rubrics (QSRs) are constructed around concrete task objectives, authored by experts, and validated through multiple rounds of cross-checking to **ensure correctness and coverage of content alignment**. Together, GRRs and QSRs **guarantee that reports meet both task completion requirements and general quality standards**, while the adjustable weighting of the Quality metric allows flexible balancing across different scenarios. This combination establishes **a complete, rigorous, and reusable evaluation framework** tailored for deep research agents.  For details on rubric coverage, please refer to Appendix B.5 for QSRs and Appendix B.2 for GRRs.

Therefore, what may appear as “dependence” is not a limitation but rather **a necessary safeguard to ensure comprehensiveness, rigor, reproducibility, and credibility** within the community.

summary.value: This paper presents a new benchmark and multidimensional evaluation framework designed for Deep Research Agents (DRAs), a class of AI systems capable of external information integration, complex reasoning and report generation. The benchmark includes 214 expert-crafted queries across 10 thematic domains, with manually curated reference materials to facilitate comprehensive evaluation. The proposed multidimensional evaluation framework assesses long-form, report-style outputs along dimensions such as semantic quality, topical relevance, and retrieval reliability.

strengths.value:
1. This work introduces a multidimensional evaluation framework that goes beyond single-metric benchmarks (like accuracy or BLEU) to assess semantic quality, topical focus, and trustworthiness.
2. The inclusion of reference bundles enables composite and contextual evaluation.

weaknesses.value:
1. The links provided in the benchmark may not work over time, as the page changes or disappears over time.
2. The motivation of compositional score metrics is not very clear. What's the difference between this work and just defining multiple fine-grained aspects and doing a performance average? Is it necessary to build such a compositional scoring framework?

questions.value:
1. Regarding the benchmark fragility and temporal decay, tasks depend on live web content (so called Trustworthy-Source Links in the paper), benchmark reproducibility decays quickly since pages change, disappear, or alter their information hierarchy. Without versioned snapshots, how to ensure these links are workable so that the proposed benchmark is useful over time?
2. What's the difference between this work and just defining multiple fine-grained aspects and doing a performance average? Is it necessary to build such a compositional scoring framework?

***(As added in Appendix B.7 of the rebuttal revision)*** Within the evaluation framework for structured long-text tasks, Query-Specific Rubrics (QSRs) constitute a dimension-based schema for assessing report completeness. Their validity and representativeness critically depend on whether they possess discriminative power for task completion and align with human user expectations. The design of QSRs considers, though is not limited to, the core dimensions summarized in Table R.1.

Table R.1: Core dimensions with descriptions of QSRs

| **Dimensions**                          | **Descriptions**                                             |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Information Coverage                    | Whether the report fully covers key facts, events, clauses, persons, institutions, or geographic units required by the query, ensuring no essential information is missing. |
| Technical / Mechanism Explanation       | Whether the report accurately explains mechanisms, protocols, causal chains, policy tools, or theoretical frameworks involved in the query, reflecting mastery of core logic. |
| Structural Expression                   | Whether the report generates structured forms such as tables, timelines, maps, matrices, or lists to support organization and reproducibility of the task. |
| Semantic Precision                      | Whether the report defines key terms, distinguishes concepts, annotates units and time, and avoids ambiguity, ensuring clarity and consistency of expression. |
| Source Verification                     | Whether the report cites authoritative texts, identifiers, database versions, retrieval times, links, or snapshots to support traceability and credibility of claims. |
| Evidence Organization                   | Whether the report employs multi-source cross-validation, independent source pairing, counterfactual baselines, placebo tests, or robustness checks to enhance reliability. |
| Heterogeneity and Comparative Analysis  | Whether the report identifies and analyzes differences across regions, groups, time periods, or institutions, supporting comparative and explanatory power. |
| Methodological Transparency             | Whether the report clearly explains analytical methods, identification strategies, variable definitions, and data processing steps, ensuring consistency and reproducibility. |
| Social Impact and Distribution Effects  | Whether the report analyzes distributional impacts of policies or events on different groups, communities, industries, or ecosystems, reflecting social dimensions. |
| Historical Evolution and Temporal Logic | Whether the report establishes event chains, policy evolution paths, time windows, or lag mechanisms, supporting historical and dynamic analysis. |
| Interdisciplinary Integration           | Whether the report integrates perspectives from multiple disciplines (e.g., law, economics, technology, society, philosophy) to support complexity and explanatory depth. |

Compared with General-Report Rubrics (GRRs), QSRs are fully query-driven. On the basis of comprehensive coverage, they further emphasize alignment with human-expected responses to specific queries, thereby demonstrating strong task relevance and diagnostic capability.

The integrated score is multiplicatively composed of three parts: Quality, SemanticDrift, and TrustworthyBoost. Table 1 provides metric-wise ablation analysis, **demonstrating the necessity of each component**.

Overall, our benchmark design is **not tailored to any specific system or stylistic preference**; rather, it **provides an objective, effective, and holistic framework** for evaluating the integrated performance of deep research agents. This benchmark establishes **a rigorous and broadly applicable standard** that can **fairly and transparently measure the true capabilities** of different systems in deep research scenarios.
